query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning surrogate model, trained on extensive experimental datasets that include hierarchical microstructural descriptors, can predict the Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure significantly faster (by roughly an order of magnitude) and with prediction errors under 15% at room temperature (and under 20% at elevated temperatures) compared to established simulation methods.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 high-entropy alloy fabricated with a controlled, hierarchical heterostructure ensuring reproducible grain size, phase distribution, and microstructural details.
generation.intervention: Application of a machine learning surrogate model that integrates elemental composition, processing history, and hierarchical microstructural features via advanced feature correlation techniques.
generation.conditions: Tensile and fracture tests performed under controlled laboratory conditions at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C), with samples prepared using established fabrication and processing protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Hierarchical heterostructural parameters (such as grain boundary density, phase composition and distribution, and defect structures captured from imaging and compositional analysis) that serve as key inputs for the ML model.
generation.mechanism: The ML surrogate leverages correlations between intrinsic HEA features and observed mechanical properties from experimental data. By effectively mapping how microstructural heterogeneity influences dislocation movement, bonding, and fracture behavior, the model enables rapid prediction of mechanical responses without the need for computationally intensive simulations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Substantially reduced computational time (approximately one-tenth of the time required by detailed finite element or atomistic simulations) coupled with mechanical property predictions (Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness) that deviate less than 15% from experimental values at room temperature and less than 20% at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Traditional simulation approaches such as finite element analysis or atomistic/molecular dynamics simulations, which require extensive computational resources and time.
generation.boundary: The surrogate model may fail when the hierarchical heterostructure exhibits unforeseen microstructural anomalies or phase transformations that are not represented within the training dataset, or under processing conditions that introduce additional variability (e.g., misalignment during testing or unexpected defect formation).
generation.uncertainty: While predicted gains in speed and accuracy are based on evidence from similar systems, exact error margins and efficiency improvements for HfNbTiVAl10 specifically remain uncertain until further targeted experimental validation is performed, particularly under varied processing histories.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTiVAl10 samples with verified hierarchical heterostructures and perform standardized tensile and fracture tests at room temperature and at selected elevated temperatures (600–800 °C). Use the machine learning surrogate model to generate predictions for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for each sample. Compare the predicted values directly with the experimentally measured values.
measurements: Young’s modulus (via stress–strain slope in the elastic regime)
Fracture toughness and strain-to-fracture (via standardized fracture testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model’s predicted values exceed an absolute error of 20% from the corresponding experimental measurements (consistently across multiple samples and conditions), then the hypothesis that the ML surrogate achieves both rapid prediction and improved accuracy over traditional simulations for HfNbTiVAl10 is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as an indispensable tool in computational materials science, offering the ability to analyze extensive datasets, identify complex patterns, and predict properties based on input features. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of ML in predicting HEA properties [,,,,,,,,,]. These studies typically involve the collection of extensive experimental data, the selection of relevant features, and the development of predictive models using various ML algorithms. For instance, Sengupta et al. [] employed a Neural Network model to predict the yield strength and plasticity of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), using elemental composition and physics-based properties as features. This study also highlighted the role of uncertainty quantification in enhancing predictive reliability.

The benefits of this work are to demonstrate that pairwise interactions independent of the elemental information largely drive phase formation and provide new physical understanding, while at the same time providing a more robust data representation, which is critical with increasing alloy complexity. It should be noted that the input data are from experimental studies, and therefore, the relationships among chemistry, processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties are all contained in the data, even if not explicitly defined. This approach adds practical considerations of the alloy beyond theoretical predictions, incorporating real-world complexity into the model. Through this, and with developed models of reasonable accuracy, we can understand the behavior of HEAs at a length scale larger than in prior studies and thus better understand the role of bonding in the resulting HEA mechanical properties.

The bagging (from bootstrap aggregating) [] approach was used for improving the prediction accuracy. To this end, 1000 datasets with a size of 0.7 of the initial datasets were randomly selected for (i) training surrogate model, (ii) yield strength prediction and (iii) calculating the average yield strength. The alloys with the yield strength less than the average value were excluded from consideration, due to which the number of the alloys was reduced to 11770. Then, the phenomenological phase formation criteria and the CALPHAD approach were used to select predominantly single-phase alloys.

All alloys showed some ductility (i.e., did not fracture in the elastic region), yet only the A1 and A5 alloys had a ductility over 5% (17.2% and 5.5%, respectively). At 800 °C, all the model alloys did not fracture till 50% height reduction. Only three model alloys (A3, A5 and A6) showed yield strength more than 300 MPa (556, 898 and 509 MPa, respectively). For other alloys, the yield strengths were in a range between 152 and 287 MPa. The best strength/ductility ratio at all tested temperatures was demonstrated by the A5 alloy.
